key_terms.meaning: H(S) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ, the average uncertainty in bits of a label set S; pᵢ is the fraction of S with label i.
Gain(S, A) = H(S) − Σᵥ (|Sᵥ|/|S|)·H(Sᵥ), the entropy drop when attribute A splits S into parts Sᵥ.
Greedy top-down tree learner that splits on the attribute with the highest information gain until a node is pure or attributes run out.
The belief that hypothesis h is correct before any data is seen.
The probability of observing the data D if hypothesis h were the true one.
P(h|D) = P(D|h)·P(h) / P(D), belief in h after seeing D.
h_MAP = argmax over h of P(D|h)·P(h); picks the most probable hypothesis after the data.
h_MLE = argmax over h of P(D|h); this is MAP with all priors treated as equal.
P(x₁, x₂ | y) = P(x₁|y)·P(x₂|y); the assumption naive Bayes makes about features.
Add-one correction (count + 1)/(total + K) so a feature never gets probability zero.
argmax over c of Σ over h of P(c|h)·P(h|D); every hypothesis votes weighted by its posterior.
Draw one hypothesis at random with probability P(h|D) and predict with that single hypothesis.
A directed acyclic graph with a conditional probability table per node, giving joint P = Π P(Xᵢ | parents(Xᵢ)).
Store all training pairs; label a query by the majority label among its k nearest stored points.
Neighbour i votes with weight 1/d(x, xᵢ) so closer points count more; ties go to the nearest.
For a hyperplane w·x + b = 0, the margin is 2/‖w‖, the total gap to the nearest points on both sides.
K(x, z) = φ(x)·φ(z) gives a dot product in a higher-dimensional space without ever computing φ explicitly.
Train many copies of a model on bootstrap samples (drawn with replacement) and average or vote their outputs.
Add models one at a time, each new one trained on the examples the current ensemble gets wrong, so bias falls.
For each query, fit a simple model using training points weighted by distance, so the fit is local, not global.

takeaways: ID3 chooses the split that removes the most entropy, and information gain is the number it maximises.
Bayes theorem turns a prior plus a likelihood into a posterior; MAP keeps the prior, MLE drops it.
Naive Bayes is fast and needs little data because it multiplies one probability per feature instead of modelling their interactions.
The Bayes optimal classifier is the best you can do given the hypothesis space, but it is usually too expensive to compute.
A Bayesian belief network stores a large joint distribution compactly as local conditional tables on a DAG.
kNN is accurate but slow at prediction time and stores the whole training set.
An SVM maximises the margin, so only the support vectors decide the boundary, and kernels make it non-linear.
Bagging and random forests average away variance; boosting drives down bias by fixing mistakes.
Local methods such as kNN, RBF networks and locally weighted regression fit the query point, not the whole dataset.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask you to state the method, write its formula, and then carry a small numeric example through to a prediction, with decision trees, naive Bayes and the SVM margin derivation appearing most often.

bank.q: Define entropy and information gain for a decision tree. Build an ID3 tree for a small table of weather attributes and a play/not-play label, showing the gain calculation at the root.
outline: Entropy formula with base-2 logs and its meaning in bits
Information gain formula, weighted by part sizes
Root gain computed for each attribute
Recursive splitting until pure leaves
Stopping rules: pure node, no attributes left, pruning

bank.q: State Bayes theorem. Explain maximum likelihood estimation and maximum a posteriori estimation, and show when they give the same answer.
outline: P(h|D) = P(D|h)P(h)/P(D), each term defined
MLE maximises only the likelihood
MAP maximises likelihood times prior
MAP equals MLE when the prior is uniform
Coin-toss or die-roll example with numbers

bank.q: Explain the naive Bayes classifier, its independence assumption, and why Laplace smoothing is needed.
outline: Classify as argmax P(c) Π P(xᵢ|c)
Conditional independence stated as a formula
Zero-frequency problem
Add-one smoothing formula
Log-space computation to avoid underflow

bank.q: Describe the Bayes optimal classifier and the Gibbs algorithm. Why is the Bayes optimal classifier rarely usable in practice?
outline: Bayes optimal averages over hypotheses weighted by posterior
Gibbs samples one hypothesis and predicts with it
Expected error of Gibbs is at most twice the Bayes optimal
Cost grows with the number of hypotheses
Both need the full posterior over the hypothesis space

bank.q: Draw a Bayesian belief network for a small domain of four or five variables and compute a joint probability from it.
outline: Nodes are variables, edges are direct dependence, graph is acyclic
One conditional probability table per node
Joint factorises into local conditionals
Number of stored values versus full joint table
Inference by enumerating hidden variables

bank.q: Compare decision trees, naive Bayes, kNN and SVM on interpretability, training cost, prediction cost, sensitivity to scaling, and ability to fit a non-linear boundary.
outline: Tree: interpretable, unstable, no scaling needed
Naive Bayes: fastest, strong independence assumption
kNN: no training, slow prediction, sensitive to scale and irrelevant features
SVM: strong on small high-dimensional data, needs tuning of C and kernel
Recommendation tied to data size, noise and need for explanation

bank.q: A small labelled dataset of emails with three binary word features is given. Apply naive Bayes with Laplace smoothing to classify a new email, showing every probability.
outline: Prior from class counts
Per-feature conditional counts with smoothing
Multiply likelihoods for the query
Compare posterior scores across classes
Note that only the ratio matters, not the evidence P(D)

bank.q: Given eight two-dimensional labelled points, classify a query point using kNN for k = 1, 3 and 5, then repeat with distance weighting. Explain any change in the answer.
outline: Euclidean distances computed and ordered
Majority vote for each k
Weight w = 1/d and weighted sums
Tie-breaking rule stated
Larger k smooths the boundary but blurs local structure

bank.q: For a two-class dataset where the closest points to a separating hyperplane are at distance 1/‖w‖ on each side, derive the maximum-margin objective and write its dual.
outline: Hyperplane w·x + b = 0 and labels yᵢ ∈ {−1, +1}
Constraints yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1
Minimise ½‖w‖² subject to those constraints
Lagrange multipliers and the dual in terms of dot products
Support vectors are the points with non-zero multipliers

bank.q: A decision tree trained on 5000 records gives 100 percent training accuracy and 78 percent test accuracy. Explain what went wrong, describe two pruning methods, and state how you would choose the pruning level.
outline: Overfitting due to deep splits on small samples
Reduced-error pruning and rule post-pruning
Validation set or cross-validation to pick subtree
Effect of minimum-samples-per-leaf
Trade-off between interpretability and accuracy

bank.q: Analyse why bagging reduces variance while boosting reduces bias. Refer to a single decision tree that is deep and unstable in one case and shallow in the other.
outline: Bias-variance decomposition of expected error
Deep trees: low bias, high variance, so averaging helps
Bootstrap samples are correlated; averaging correlated predictors still cuts variance
Boosting adds capacity in sequence, so it lowers bias
Boosting can overfit noisy labels, bagging rarely does

bank.q: A hospital wants a classifier for a rare disease from 2000 records with 40 features and must justify each decision to doctors. Evaluate naive Bayes, kNN, an SVM with an RBF kernel and a random forest for this task, and recommend one.
outline: Class imbalance and why accuracy misleads; use precision, recall, F1
Naive Bayes with Gaussian features gives probabilities and is cheap
kNN poor with 40 features and imbalance
SVM needs scaling and tuning of C and γ, gives no explanation
Random forest gives feature importance and handles imbalance with weighting

bank.q: Explain the kernel trick. Show how a polynomial kernel of degree 2 maps two-dimensional data into three dimensions, and discuss how the choice of kernel and C controls overfitting.
outline: Explicit feature map φ and its cost
K(x, z) = (x·z + 1)² expanded into three features
Mercer condition for a valid kernel
Large C: narrow margin, low bias, high variance
Kernel width γ and its effect on the boundary

bank.q: Compare instance-based learning with eager learning. Discuss the curse of dimensionality for kNN and explain how locally weighted regression and RBF networks soften the problem.
outline: kNN stores data, no explicit model, lazy prediction
Distance concentration in high dimensions
Locally weighted regression fits a weighted model per query
RBF network places Gaussian bumps at centres and learns output weights
Case-based reasoning reuses past cases through adaptation rather than averaging

glossary.def: A measure of the impurity of a labelled set, zero when all labels agree and largest when they are evenly mixed.
The expected reduction in entropy obtained by splitting a set on one attribute.
The attribute chosen at a tree node, namely the one with the highest information gain or lowest Gini impurity.
Removing unhelpful subtrees from a grown tree to reduce overfitting on unseen data.
The probability assigned to a hypothesis or class before any evidence is observed.
The probability of the observed data under a given hypothesis, treated as a function of the hypothesis.
The updated probability of a hypothesis after the data is taken into account.
The term P(D) in Bayes theorem, a normalising constant that makes posteriors sum to one.
Choosing the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable, ignoring the prior.
Choosing the parameter or hypothesis with the largest posterior probability.
A classifier that multiplies a class prior by per-feature likelihoods, assuming features are independent given the class.
Adding a small count to every feature value so that unseen combinations do not get probability zero.
The classifier that predicts the class with the highest posterior probability averaged over all hypotheses.
A randomised learner that samples one hypothesis by its posterior and predicts with that hypothesis only.
A directed acyclic graph whose nodes are random variables and whose edges encode direct conditional dependence.
The table at a network node listing the probability of each value of that node for every combination of its parents.
A classifier that assigns a query the majority label among the k stored training points closest to it.
The partition of the feature space into regions, each region holding the points closer to one training example than to any other.
The loss of meaning of distance as dimensions grow, because points become almost equidistant from each other.
A training point that lies on or inside the margin and therefore fixes the SVM boundary.
The distance between the separating hyperplane and the closest training points on either side, equal to 2/‖w‖.
A similarity function that equals a dot product in some feature space, letting a linear method act non-linearly.
A sample of the same size as the training set, drawn with replacement so some rows appear more than once.
A collection of decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample and split on a random subset of features, combined by vote.
A boosting algorithm that reweights misclassified examples upward and gives each weak learner a vote based on its accuracy.
Solving a new problem by retrieving a similar stored case and adapting its known solution.
